sentences: Here is a morning at a Joseon village school.
The pupils sit in a ring around their teacher, and in the middle one small boy crouches, wiping away tears.
First, take in the mood of the whole room.
The painter is Kim Hong-do, known as Danwon, of late Joseon Korea.
He joined the royal painting bureau at twenty-one and handled the court's major commissions for decades.
Yet he loved to paint the everyday lives of ordinary people like these.
Up above, the teacher sits behind a low desk, looking down at the boy.
His face wears a look somewhere between awkward and sorry.
Some even read it as a man trying not to laugh himself.
Look at the boy just in front of the teacher.
He seems to have stumbled in a recitation, the kind of test where you recite with the book behind your back.
Crying, he tugs his trouser hem down over a freshly switched calf.
Now move your eyes to the pupils sitting in a row on the left.
They cover their mouths or twist away, trying hard to hold back a laugh.
Laughter that will not stay down, right beside a friend's tears, is oddly endearing.
The pupils below also turn toward the boy, each with a different expression.
With one crying child between them, nearly everyone in the room is holding in a smile.
One boy's tears and many people's laughter share a single page.
There are almost no walls or windows in this picture.
Kim Hong-do paints almost no background at all: the gestures and the folds of the robes carry the whole room.
So our eyes stay on the people alone.
The ink lines that form the folds change from thick to thin as they sweep past.
Only a light wash of colour is laid on top, yet you can feel the weight and movement of seated bodies.
That is the charm of ink with light colour.
This leaf, about the size of two open hands, is one of twenty-five in his famous Genre Album.
The album is designated a Treasure and is kept at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Perhaps the scene is loved because scolding and laughter, hurt and warmth are all held in one moment.
It lets us imagine what the village school was like for the children who studied there, and this genre painting keeps that memory alive.
Finally, step back and imagine yourself in the crying boy's place.
His friends' laughter must have stung terribly that day.
But as the years went by, might it not have become a fond memory?
